source.title: More than a Metric: How Training Load is Used in Elite Sport for Athlete Management

paper.citation: West, S. W., Clubb, J., Torres-Ronda, L., Howells, D., Leng, E., Vescovi, J. D., Carmody, S., Posthumus, M., Dalen-Lorentsen, T., & Windt, J. (2021). More than a metric: How training load is used in elite sport for athlete management. International Journal of Sports Medicine, 42(4), 300–306. https://doi.org/10.1055/a-1268-8791
paper.abstract: How can elite-sport practitioners use training-load information across immediate feedback, session adjustment, day-to-day planning, season planning, and long-term athlete management without reducing complex decisions to one metric? This is a peer-reviewed editorial informed by the authors’ experience across multiple team and individual sports, not an empirical study with participants or measured outcomes. Examples include association football, American football, basketball, rugby, baseball, and other sports, so propositions remain context dependent. The authors synthesize selected literature, conceptual models, and practitioner experience to describe uses, constraints, and communication needs in training-load monitoring. No systematic search, formal consensus process, risk-of-bias assessment, or empirical evaluation is reported.
paper.tldr: This editorial reframes training-load monitoring as a contextual, multi-timescale decision process rather than an injury-prediction metric, with direct relevance to how performance departments collect, interpret, and communicate athlete data. Editorial proposition, not an empirical finding: tools are valuable when they provide sufficiently accurate information for a defined performance decision while minimizing athlete and practitioner burden. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: The authors synthesize selected literature, conceptual models, and practitioner experience to describe uses, constraints, and communication needs in training-load monitoring. No systematic search, formal consensus process, risk-of-bias assessment, or empirical evaluation is reported.
paper.findings: Editorial proposition, not an empirical finding: tools are valuable when they provide sufficiently accurate information for a defined performance decision while minimizing athlete and practitioner burden. External and internal load should be interpreted within a model connecting data to a desired outcome; validity, reliability, and utility require evaluation in the intended environment. The authors explicitly reject any single metric or metric collection as a definitive injury-prediction tool and describe causal links between load and injury as unresolved. Load data may support five levels of use: feedback, in-session adjustment, day-to-day planning, season planning, and long-term athlete management. Individual athlete, match, travel, environmental, psychological, career-stage, and organizational context can change interpretation; communication and interdepartmental collaboration are therefore part of the monitoring process. Monitoring systems should surface critical cues, filter irrelevant data, support staff work, and track progress toward defined goals.
paper.limitations: The paper is an expert editorial; it does not demonstrate that its framework improves performance, reduces injury, or outperforms alternative decision processes. Selected examples and citations cannot establish prevalence, causal effects, or universal best practice. Assertions that rest may reduce useful exposure or that strategic overload improves outcomes require sport-, tissue-, athlete-, and phase-specific evidence rather than automatic application. Wearables may miss isometric and contact loads relevant to American-football linemen, and technology restrictions or missing data can distort the observed workload. Athlete monitoring cannot reveal the counterfactual outcome of a decision to train, modify, or rest, which creates hindsight and attribution bias.
paper.practicalImplications: For collegiate American football, define the intended decision before selecting metrics, validate data quality locally, and pair physical-load data with role, drill, contact, tactical, medical, and athlete-reported context. Use monitoring to prepare athletes for demands and review progression, not to produce a single “risk” score. Make uncertainty and missing load visible, especially for linemen and contact work, and communicate recommendations in language coaches and athletes can interrogate.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. For collegiate American football, define the intended decision before selecting metrics, validate data quality locally, and pair physical-load data with role, drill, contact, tactical, medical, and athlete-reported context. paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
